records.place: Wachenheim, with the vineyard at Forst, Mittelhaardt, Pfalz

wine.name: Forster Kirchenstück G.C.
wine.classification: G.C., the estate's own Grand Cru rank; the site is a VDP.Grosse Lage
wine.sites: The Kirchenstück, a small vineyard beside the church of Forst ringed by a knee high sandstone wall: a gentle east and south east slope on basalt, sandstone, limestone rubble and clay over a limestone plate.
wine.making: From vines the estate began to farm biodynamically in 2005. Like every G.C. wine of the house, it ferments with wild yeasts and is raised only in large oak casks before it is bottled dry.
wine.glass: White peach, lime zest and pink grapefruit over wet stone and a faint smoky note; dry, taut and finely textured, with bright acidity, a salty grip and a long, tightly wound finish.
wine.ageing: Reserved for its first five years or so, it opens slowly and keeps for twenty years and more in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large white wine glass.

label.means: Grand Cru: the highest rank in the estate's own classification of its vineyards, not a term of German wine law.
The church piece: the walled vineyard beside the church of Forst.
The Mittelhaardt village between Wachenheim and Deidesheim where the Kirchenstück lies.

records.table: Dr. Bürklin-Wolf's Forster Kirchenstück G.C. is dry Riesling from a small walled vineyard beside the church at Forst, the site that, by the estate's account, a Bavarian survey of 1828 placed above every other. Fermented with wild yeasts in large casks, it is taut, smoky and long.
records.story: The house traces its roots in Wachenheim to 1597, and its history names a Bürklin of that age, a town clerk who became mayor of Wachenheim. The modern estate began with a marriage. In 1875 Albert Bürklin (1844 to 1924), a lawyer and member of the Reichstag, married a daughter of the Wolf family of Wachenheim, and her family's vineyards in Wachenheim, Forst, Deidesheim and Ruppertsberg came together under both names. He moved to Wachenheim and built the estate up. In 1924 it passed to a great nephew of the same name, Albert Bürklin (1907 to 1979), who by the estate's account led the rebuilding of Pfalz wine after the Second World War and added vineyards and cellars; his eldest daughter inherited in 1990. Long before, in 1828, a royal Bavarian survey had ranked the vineyards of the Pfalz for land tax, and the estate records that the Kirchenstück alone received the highest mark. In the 1990s the house made that survey the base of its own ladder, in the manner of Burgundy, printing G.C. and P.C. on its labels, and in 2005 it began to farm biodynamically. For a sommelier the Kirchenstück is the summit of that ladder: a small walled vineyard read as a Grand Cru, though German law knows no such word.

Bürklin-Wolf, von Buhl and Bassermann-Jordan are the three historic Mittelhaardt estates candidates confuse; Bürklin-Wolf is the one at Wachenheim.
The Kirchenstück of Forst in the Pfalz is not the Kirchenstück of Hohen-Sülzen in Rheinhessen, a separate site on limestone and loess.

Andreas Jordan, the Deidesheim grower of 1802
Franz Peter Buhl, founder of a Deidesheim estate

report: Read through search summaries of the estate's own history and terroir pages and its shop page for the Kirchenstück G.C., the VDP's page on the site, and secondary accounts (Wein.plus, Skurnik, Vinello, the VIAF and Archivportal-D records for Albert Bürklin's dates); 6 of the author's 35 searches went to this house.

The making rests on the estate's terroir page, which says every G.C. wine is fermented with wild yeasts and raised only in large oak casks; no sheet for the Kirchenstück alone gave a cask size or a time in wood, so none is given.
The year the estate began its own ranking is 1990 on its terroir page and 1994 in Wein.plus and Skurnik, so the story says the 1990s; 2005 for biodynamics rests on Skurnik and Vinello.

Luise Wolf's dates (1848 to 1882) were found in one source only, so she is described, not named; the Bürklin of 1597, a town clerk and mayor whom the estate dates 1580 to 1636, is described because the estate alone gives him.
That the 1828 survey gave the Kirchenstück alone its highest mark is the estate's claim, told as the estate records it; the library's wine note says the same.

The library's trap that Forst's basalt was quarried and spread is borne out for the Pechstein by the VDP's page, which names a nineteenth century quarry; the library writes Kirchenstuck without its umlaut in holdings and traps.
The eldest daughter who inherited in 1990 is living and listed in people.json, so she is described.

records.place: Deidesheim, Mittelhaardt, Pfalz; the vineyard lies at Forst

wine.name: Forster Jesuitengarten Riesling Grosses Gewächs
wine.classification: VDP.Grosses Gewächs: the dry wine of a VDP.Grosse Lage, the association's highest site rank
wine.sites: The Jesuitengarten at Forst, named for the old Jesuit house of Neustadt that owned it, on sandy loam, sandstone rubble, marly clay and basalt.
wine.making: The grapes are pressed gently and the must is split: part ferments with the vineyard's own yeasts in traditional oak Stückfass casks, part in stainless steel. Both stay on their lees until bottling, and the wine is bottled dry.
wine.glass: Ripe yellow peach, orange zest and pear over honeysuckle and a smoky, stony thread; dry yet broad and juicy, more perfume than grip, with ripe acidity and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Open and generous within a few years of the vintage, it keeps and deepens for fifteen years and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; half an hour in a decanter opens a young bottle; a large white wine glass.

label.means: Privy councillor, an honorary title of the old German states, kept in the estate's name.
Great growth: the dry wine the VDP allows only from a site it ranks Grosse Lage.
The Jesuits' garden, a Forst vineyard once owned by the Jesuits of Neustadt.

records.table: Bassermann-Jordan's Forster Jesuitengarten Riesling is a dry Grosses Gewächs from a Forst vineyard named for the Jesuits who once owned it, fermented partly in traditional oak casks with its own yeasts. Broad, ripe and gently smoky, it suits roast pork or river fish.
records.story: By the estate's account its story begins in 1718, when a Jordan forebear founded it. Its maker was Andreas Jordan (1775 to 1848), who took it over at twenty after his parents' deaths and built a house of quality from shrinking assets. He is credited with selling, from 1802, Pfalz wine named for its village and its vineyard. He died in 1848 without a will, and his estate was divided equally among his three children; from the shares came three houses, Jordan, Buhl and Deinhard, the last of them the estate that became von Winning. Under the Bassermann-Jordan name two brothers ran the house together, the younger Friedrich von Bassermann-Jordan (1872 to 1959), who published a history of viticulture in three volumes in 1907 and led the Bavarian wine growers' association. The vaulted cellar beneath the estate keeps old vintages back to 1811. In 2002 the estate was sold to a Neustadt entrepreneur. For a sommelier the Jesuitengarten carries the Jordan inheritance in one glass: a Forst site, a house of 1718, and the habit of naming a wine for its vineyard.

others.name: Forster Kirchenstück Riesling Grosses Gewächs
others.note: The house's wine from the small walled vineyard beside the church of Forst.

others.name: Forster Ungeheuer Riesling Grosses Gewächs
others.note: Its Grosses Gewächs from the Ungeheuer, another Forst site.

traps: Bassermann-Jordan, von Buhl and von Winning all grew from one estate, Andreas Jordan's, divided among his three children after his death in 1848.
The Jesuitengarten of Forst in the Pfalz is not the Jesuitengarten of Winkel in the Rheingau, an alluvial site named for the Jesuit college of Mainz.
Geheimer Rat in the estate's name is a title, privy councillor, not a vineyard or a style of wine.

cards.front: Bassermann-Jordan: how far back do the vintages in its cellar run?

cards.front: Which three Mittelhaardt estates grew out of the Jordan inheritance of 1848?
cards.back: Bassermann-Jordan, Reichsrat von Buhl and the Deinhard estate that became von Winning.

questions.q: A guest asks why the Forst vineyard behind Bassermann-Jordan's Grosses Gewächs is called the Jesuitengarten. What do you say?
opts: It once was land of the Jesuit house of Neustadt
Jesuit monks first planted Riesling in the Pfalz there
Its wine was served at the Jesuit college of Mainz
Jesuits walled it after the Thirty Years War

questions.q: Andreas Jordan died in 1848 without a will. What became of his Deidesheim estate?
opts: It was divided equally among his three children
It passed whole to the Jesuits of Neustadt
It was sold at auction to a Bavarian bank
It went to his steward, who renamed it
questions.exp: With no will, the estate was split equally among his three children, and from the shares came the Jordan, Buhl and Deinhard estates; it never passed whole to anyone.

report: Read through search summaries of the estate's own pages (Pioniergeist, Herkunft and the shop sheets of the 2024 and 2025 Jesuitengarten), the VDP's site page and secondary accounts (Wein.plus, Meininger, KuLaDig, the Rheinland-Pfälzische Bibliographie, the history society GGW, Decanter, Wines of Germany); 6 of the author's 35 searches went to this house.

The estate names its founder of 1718 Pierre Jordan, while the KuLaDig monument record names a Johann Peter Jordan with dates (1753 to 1795) that cannot fit 1718, so the founder is described as a Jordan forebear.

Andreas Jordan's dates rest on the estate's own page and KuLaDig; the sale of wine by village and vineyard from 1802 is in two accounts (Wines of Germany and Wein.plus) and is told as a credit, not a proven first.
The elder brother, Ludwig (1869 to 1914), has dates in one source only and is described; Friedrich's dates are in Wein.plus and the regional bibliography, his book of 1907 in Wein.plus and the GGW.
The cellar's vintages back to 1811 rest on Meininger, KuLaDig and an importer; Decanter's report of an 1811 Forster Ungeheuer opened for the three hundredth year is one source and is left out.

Left out for want of a second source: the family's purchase of the Jesuitengarten in 1793 (the estate's Herkunft page alone), the move to Deidesheim in 1783 (KuLaDig alone), and the buyer's name, a man who died in 2013, given in one record only with dates.
The house is not in the library; the estate's sheets give the cask and steel split as part and part, varying by vintage, so no share is given.

wine.name: Forster Pechstein Riesling Grosses Gewächs
wine.classification: VDP.Grosses Gewächs from the Pechstein, a VDP.Grosse Lage of Forst
wine.sites: The Pechstein at Forst, named for its black basalt: rubble from the Pechsteinkopf, an old volcano above the slope, mixed with weathered red sandstone and clay, and basalt from a nearby quarry spread in the nineteenth century.
wine.making: Fermented with native yeasts, mostly in the Doppelstück, the 2400 litre oak cask of the region, with a small part in stainless steel, then aged on its fine lees before it is bottled dry.
wine.glass: Smoke, struck flint and crushed stone over lime, white peach and lemon peel; dry and taut, darker and more savoury than its Forst neighbours, with firm acidity and a salty finish.
wine.ageing: Closed and smoky in youth, it opens after five years or so and keeps for fifteen to twenty.
wine.serve: 11 to 12 degrees Celsius; an hour in a decanter helps a young bottle; a tall white wine glass.

label.means: A title borne by the Buhl family and kept in the estate's name.
Pitch stone: the vineyard named for the black basalt in its soil.
Short for Grosses Gewächs, the VDP's dry wine from a Grosse Lage.

records.table: Reichsrat von Buhl's Forster Pechstein Riesling grows on the black basalt of an old volcano above Forst and ferments with its own yeasts in large oak casks. Dry, smoky and taut, darker voiced than its Forst neighbours, it wants grilled fish.
records.story: When Andreas Jordan died in 1848, his Deidesheim estate was divided among his three children, and in 1849 Franz Peter Buhl (1809 to 1862) founded this house with one of the three shares. His son, Franz Armand Buhl (1837 to 1896), inherited it and carried the name into politics: elected to the Reichstag in 1871, he sat there until 1893, and the wine law it passed in the early 1890s owed much to his initiative. The title of Reichsrat, borne by the family, stayed in the estate's name. In 1989 the estate was leased to a Japanese businessman, a lease that ran until 2013; during it, in 2005, the estate was sold to a Neustadt entrepreneur, and when the lease ended a new team took over the cellar. Forst lies at the heart of the house, and its own pages quote the old line that whoever has not been to Buhl does not know Forst Riesling. The Pechstein, its basalt shed by the Pechsteinkopf and spread from a quarry, gives a darker, smokier wine than its neighbours. A sommelier pours it beside a Kirchenstück or a Jesuitengarten to show what basalt adds to Forst.

others.name: von Buhl Riesling Brut
others.note: Traditional method Sekt of Riesling, the sparkling wine the house is also known for.

others.name: Forster Kirchenstück Riesling Grosses Gewächs
others.note: The estate's wine from the Kirchenstück, the walled site by the church of Forst.

others.name: Forster Freundstück Riesling Grosses Gewächs
others.note: Another Forst Grosse Lage the estate bottles on its own.

traps: Reichsrat von Buhl is a Deidesheim estate, though its Pechstein lies in the next village, Forst.
Von Buhl, Bassermann-Jordan and von Winning share one origin, the Jordan estate divided after 1848; von Buhl dates from 1849.
The Pechstein's basalt is partly native, from the Pechsteinkopf, and partly spread from a quarry in the nineteenth century.

cards.front: Reichsrat von Buhl's Pechstein: what gives the vineyard its name?
cards.back: Its black basalt, from the Pechsteinkopf, an old volcano above Forst; Pech means pitch.

cards.front: Which Buhl sat in the Reichstag from 1871 and pressed for a wine law in the early 1890s?
cards.back: Franz Armand Buhl (1837 to 1896), son of the founder of Reichsrat von Buhl.

questions.q: A guest asks why Reichsrat von Buhl's Forster Pechstein tastes smokier than other Forst Rieslings. Which reason fits?
opts: Black basalt from an old volcano in its soil
Charred new barriques used for its fermentation
Grapes dried on straw mats before pressing
Late picking with a large share of noble rot
questions.exp: The Pechstein is named for its basalt, from the Pechsteinkopf volcano and a nineteenth century quarry; the wine ferments in large Doppelstück casks, not charred new barriques.

questions.q: Reichsrat von Buhl was founded at Deidesheim in 1849. From what did it come?
opts: One of three shares of the divided Jordan estate
A Jesuit house of Neustadt closed by the state
A growers' cooperative founded after a war
The Bavarian crown's own cellar in the Pfalz
questions.exp: Andreas Jordan's estate was divided among his three children after his death in 1848, and Franz Peter Buhl founded the house with one share; Jesuit land gave the Jesuitengarten its name, not this estate.

report: Read through search summaries of the estate's own page, the VDP's site page, the Deutsche Biographie, a mirror copy of the Wikipedia article (cited at its Wikipedia address), KuLaDig and two importers' sheets (SommSelect and a Mundi sheet); 6 of the author's 35 searches went to this house, one of them wasted.

The making rests on SommSelect (spontaneous fermentation in the Doppelstück, fine lees) and the Mundi sheet (the main part in Doppelstück, a small part in steel); no estate sheet was found, and the bottling in the summer after the harvest, in one source, is left out.

The sources disagree on who received the title Reichsrat and when (Franz Armand under the Bavarian crown, or his son with the name added in 1912), so the record says only that the family bore it; the son, Franz Eberhard (1867 to 1921), has dates in one source and is not named.

Left out for want of a source: the wines at the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 and Bismarck's friendship (one source), the organic certification (2009 and 2015 both given), and the Champagne cellar master of 2013 to 2019 (named only in a writer's own site and a blog).

Living or unsettled names met and kept out: the Japanese lessee, named in one source, the cellar master from Champagne, and the present winemaker; the buyer of 2005 died in 2013 and is described, his dates being in one record only.
The plan's 'Forster Pechstein Riesling' is kept as the name; labels and shops print it as Pechstein GG with Forst or Forster, and the record's label lists only Reichsrat, Pechstein and GG.

records.place: Haardt, Neustadt an der Weinstrasse, Pfalz

wine.name: Rieslaner Auslese Herzog
wine.classification: Prädikatswein, Auslese: selected ripe bunches, from the Herzog, a VDP.Erste Lage
wine.grapes: Rieslaner alone, a crossing of Silvaner and Riesling bred in Franconia in 1921.
wine.sites: The Herzog at Haardt, on the edge of Neustadt, a VDP.Erste Lage on Haardt sandstone, where the estate grows the Rieslaner for its sweet wines.
wine.making: Picked by hand, with a share of noble rot in many years, then fermented cool in stainless steel so that the fruit and the grape's high acidity stay bright; the wine is bottled sweet, at a moderate alcohol.
wine.glass: Mango, ripe peach and lime over honey, eucalyptus and dried hay, with a mushroomy touch of noble rot; sweet and full, cut through by vivid acidity, with a long, clean, tangy finish.
wine.ageing: Lovely young for its fruit, it keeps and deepens for many years, its high acidity holding the sweetness in line.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small white wine glass and a small pour.

label.means: The grape: a crossing of Silvaner and Riesling, not a kind of Riesling.
Selected harvest: the Prädikat for very ripe bunches, here made as a sweet wine.
The vineyard at Haardt, an Erste Lage in the VDP's ranking of sites.

records.table: Müller-Catoir's Rieslaner Auslese Herzog is a sweet wine of Rieslaner, a crossing of Silvaner and Riesling, grown on sandstone at Haardt. Mango, peach and honey ride on piercing acidity, so it can close a meal with a fruit tart.
records.story: The Catoirs, a Huguenot family, have grown wine at Haardt since 1744 by the estate's account, and the estate believes they had probably worked vines in France before they came. In the years around 1900 the family manor at Haardt was enlarged in the neoclassical style. In 1968 an heir took over an estate split by inheritance and, over some forty years, brought it back into one hand; with his long serving cellar master he raised its standing. They gave as much care to Scheurebe, Muskateller and Rieslaner as to Riesling, and the wines they made were vivid and aromatic. Rieslaner was bred in Franconia in 1921 from Silvaner and Riesling; it keeps high acidity, catches noble rot readily, and is grown mainly in Franconia and the Pfalz. The estate grows it in the Herzog and bottles it as Auslese, Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese, a ladder of sweetness from one site. For a sommelier it answers the question that moves past Riesling: a German sweet wine from a crossing rather than from Riesling itself.

others.name: Bürgergarten Riesling
others.note: Dry Riesling from the deep soil of the Bürgergarten at Haardt, a VDP.Erste Lage.

others.name: Scheurebe Kabinett
others.note: Grapefruit and blackcurrant leaf, the Pfalz aromatic the house takes as seriously as Riesling.

others.name: Rieslaner Trockenbeerenauslese Herzog
others.note: Shrivelled noble rot berries from the same site, at a tiny yield.

traps: Rieslaner is a crossing of Silvaner and Riesling, not a clone or a style of Riesling.
Müller-Catoir has no link to Müller-Thurgau, whatever the shared name.
The estate's Rieslaner comes from the Herzog, not the Bürgergarten, which gives its dry Riesling.

cards.front: Müller-Catoir's Rieslaner: what are the grape's two parents?

cards.front: In which Haardt vineyard does Müller-Catoir grow the Rieslaner for its sweet wines?

Yes: a clone of Riesling chosen for sweet wine

No: a crossing of Riesling and Bukettraube

questions.q: Müller-Catoir has been in one family's hands since 1744. From what background did that family come?
opts: A Huguenot family with roots in France
A Jesuit house of Neustadt
A Bavarian noble line from Munich
A Swiss family of grape breeders

report: SWAP PROPOSED, of the wine and not the house: the plan's 'Haardter Bürgergarten Rieslaner' is not the bottling the estate leads with. Its own pages sell its Rieslaner as 'Rieslaner Auslese Herzog' (and Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese Herzog) from the Haardter Herzog, a VDP.Erste Lage on Haardt sandstone, and an importer (Bibendum) says the long serving cellar master planted Rieslaner in the Herzog; the Bürgergarten, a VDP.Erste Lage by the estate's vineyard page, gives its dry Riesling, and a Bürgergarten Rieslaner appears only as an old Beerenauslese on Vivino.

This record is therefore written for 'Rieslaner Auslese Herzog', and the lint's two problems on this record (wine.name and the table not holding the plan's words) stand until the chunk's checker agrees and changes the pick's wine in plan.json to 'Rieslaner Auslese Herzog'; the key and producerId need not change.

Read through search summaries of the estate's own About, vineyard, product and press pages, Wikipedia and Wein.plus on the grape, the Bibendum and Skurnik listings; 6 of the author's 35 searches went to this house.

The library's p-muller-catoir lists 'Haardter Bürgergarten Riesling GG' as the leading dry wine, but the estate's own vineyard page lists the Bürgergarten as a VDP.Erste Lage, from which a Grosses Gewächs cannot come; the library's wine list gives 'Rieslaner Auslese' with no site, which this record names.

The heir who took over in 1968 died in 2023 and his birth year was not found, so he is described; the cellar master of 1962 to 2002 (dates from one importer) is described, his living status not settled; the founder named on the estate's page, Johann Wilhelm Catoir, has no dates and is not named; the present owner is living and not named.

Left out for want of a second source: that the cellar master brought Rieslaner to the estate, Rieslaner's release for the Pfalz in 1968 (the estate's press page alone), an exact Auslese must weight and a time on the lees.

records.place: Schweigen, Pfalz, from vines across the border at Wissembourg in Alsace

wine.name: Spätburgunder Kammerberg Grosses Gewächs
wine.classification: VDP.Grosses Gewächs from the Kammerberg, a VDP.Grosse Lage
wine.grapes: Spätburgunder, the German name for Pinot Noir, alone.
wine.sites: The Kammerberg, part of the Schweigener Sonnenberg on the French side of the border: a steep slope facing south towards Wissembourg, 200 to 250 metres up, on weathered limestone, loam and clay over pure limestone.
wine.making: The berries are destemmed and fermented in open vats; the mash is then carried to the press by hand and pressed gently. The wine matures slowly in young oak barriques before bottling.
wine.glass: Sour cherry, wild strawberry and red currant over clove, smoke and a cool, chalky stoniness; fine grained and taut, with fresh acidity, toast from the barrique in youth and a long, savoury close.
wine.ageing: Tight and marked by its oak for its first five years, it opens with time in bottle and lasts fifteen years and more.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: The German name for Pinot Noir; later labels may print Pinot Noir instead.
The initials under which later labels of the estate name the Kammerberg.
The VDP's dry wine from one of its Grosse Lage sites, often printed GG.

records.table: Friedrich Becker's Spätburgunder Kammerberg grows on limestone just across the border in Alsace, yet it is sold as Pfalz wine from Schweigen. Destemmed, fermented in open vats and raised in young barriques, it is cherry fruited, chalky and taut.
records.story: For generations the Beckers of Schweigen ran a mixed farm on the southern edge of the Pfalz, and after the war the village's growers founded a cooperative to set winemaking going again. In 1973 the son who took over stopped selling grapes to that cooperative and filled the first bottles under the family's own name, with a fox on the label that soon became the estate's mark. He turned to Spätburgunder, which the estate says has grown on these limestone slopes for centuries. Those slopes are the heart of the story. The vineyards between Schweigen and Wissembourg changed their nationality so often that they were called Wechsellagen, and the Schweigener Sonnenberg runs over the border into France; grapes from its French side may be sold as German wine, though not the other way round. The Kammerberg lies on that side. Benedictine monks of the abbey at Wissembourg once kept Kammerweine from it in their cellar; the site then lay forgotten until 1965, when, by the VDP's account, the Beckers took it up again. A sommelier keeps it for a favourite trap: a German Grosses Gewächs grown in France.

traps: The Kammerberg lies in France, at Wissembourg, yet the wine is labelled Pfalz: grapes from the French side of the Sonnenberg may be sold as German wine.
Spätburgunder is Pinot Noir under its German name, not a late harvest wine.
Kammerberg and Sankt Paul are parcels within the Schweigener Sonnenberg, not villages of their own.

cards.front: Friedrich Becker's Kammerberg: in which country do its vines grow?
cards.back: France: on the French side of the Schweigener Sonnenberg, facing Wissembourg; the wine is sold as Pfalz.

cards.front: What changed at the Becker estate of Schweigen in 1973?
cards.back: The family stopped selling grapes to the village cooperative and filled its first bottles, with the fox on the label.

questions.q: A guest is surprised that a Pfalz Spätburgunder from Friedrich Becker grows in France. What explains the Kammerberg's label?

The vines were moved from Alsace to Schweigen in 1973

questions.exp: The Kammerberg is part of the Schweigener Sonnenberg on the French side, and its grapes may be sold as German wine; the reverse is not allowed, and the vines were never moved.

questions.exp: The VDP records that Benedictine monks of the abbey at Wissembourg kept Kammerweine in their cellar; Eberbach was the Cistercians' abbey in the Rheingau, far to the north.

sources.title: The Irish Times: Run for the border wine

report: Read through search summaries of the estate's own family, welcome and red wine pages, the VDP's pages on the Kammerberg and on the estate, and secondary accounts (The Irish Times and Meininger on the border rule, Rudi Wiest Selections and Discover Germany on the cooperative, Wein.plus on the Sonnenberg's parcels, Falstaff and Symbolic Wines on the KB label, Le Baroudeur du Vin on the barrels); 7 of the author's 35 searches went to this house.

founded is 1973, the year the family began to bottle its own wine, on the estate's page and two importers' accounts; the family farmed here for generations before, so the founding is that of the wine estate, and a checker may prefer it empty.

The founder is not named: one source (weinkenner.de) reports his death on 25 February 2025 at 77 and a second search did not confirm it, so his status is not settled; his son, who has run the estate since 2005, is living. The house keeps its name, Friedrich Becker, as a house.

The barrique's length is not given: Falstaff lists 24 months for the KB of 2020 alone, and the share of whole bunches (one retailer) is left out; the estate's own page gives destemming, open vats, hand pressing and young oak.

The legal basis of the border rule was not found in a primary text; The Irish Times and Meininger both report that the French side may be sold as German and not the reverse, so the record states the rule without naming a law.

The plan's wording 'Spätburgunder Kammerberg' is kept as the name, though older labels print 'Schweigener Kammerberg Spätburgunder' and later ones 'KB'; the integrator may prefer 'Kammerberg Spätburgunder' in plan.json.
The VDP says the site was rediscovered in 1965 by Friedrich Becker without saying which; the record says the Beckers.
